text.hook:
std::optional allocates nothing of its own.
And assigning to a full one keeps the old object alive.

The mental model for optional and expected, plus 6 myths. Swipe ➜
text.body:
Inside:
1. A value plus a flag, in place
2. How an empty optional compares
3. What happens to the T inside
4. expected: a value or a typed error
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Where the value lives, what happens when it is empty, and how to return errors without exceptions.

slides.title: A value, plus what happens without one

cards.label: optional<T> (C++17)
cards.text: A `T` or nothing: storage for one `T` **inside** the object, plus an engaged flag.

cards.label: expected<T, E> (C++23)
cards.text: A `T` or the reason why not: the empty state carries an error of type `E`.

cards.label: Value types
cards.text: Copying copies the contents. No sharing, no reference counting, no heap of their own.

slides.takeaway: Absence or failure becomes part of the **type**: the caller cannot use the result without seeing it.

slides.title: The T lives in place
slides.takeaway: Constructing an optional never allocates. The `T` itself may (a long string). Exact sizes are not fixed by the standard.

slides.title: An empty `o` compares less than everything
slides.takeaway: `std::max(a, b)` prefers any engaged optional over an empty one, which can hide missing data.

slides.title: What happens to the T inside
rows: Destroy the `T`. The optional lives on, empty
slides.takeaway: A `T&` taken from `*o` dies with the `T`, not with the optional.

slides.title: A value, or a typed error

cards.label: expected<void, E>
cards.text: Success carries nothing. A good fit for save, send or validate.

slides.takeaway: `e.error()` on a success is UB. `e.value()` on an error throws `bad_expected_access<E>`.

slides.title: Which error mechanism?
rows: Expected failures with a reason: parsers, validation, I/O
Legacy only: easy to forget the check
slides.takeaway: C++23 chains: `and_then` when the step may fail, `transform` when it always succeeds, `or_else` to recover.

items.truth: The `T` lives inside the optional object. No allocation of its own.
It adds a flag plus padding: `optional<int>` is 8 bytes (GCC, x86-64).
It destroys the contained `T`. The optional lives on, empty.

items.myth: "Assigning to an engaged optional destroys the old value first."
items.truth: It uses `T`'s assignment. Only `emplace` destroys, then constructs.
It does not compile before C++26. Use `T*`.

items.myth: "`expected` is just optional with a string."
items.truth: `E` is any type (an enum, a struct), with `error()` and `transform_error`.

slides.hero:
optional: a value or nothing.
expected: a value
or the reason why not.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The cache already holds a value.
So the fallback never runs. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: A one-liner that shows up in every config and cache lookup.

slides.title: The cache is warm. What prints?

slides.verdict_sub: `fetch()` runs on every iteration, cache hit or not
bullets: `value_or` is an ordinary function: its argument is evaluated **before** the call.
`cache` is engaged, so the fetched string is thrown away. Three times.
Optimization level does not change it: the call has side effects.
`value_or` is fine for cheap defaults like `0` or `""`.
slides.wrong: "A: the default is only evaluated when the optional is empty"

slides.title: Make the fallback lazy
slides.tip: Both versions leave `fetches=0` for a warm cache.
slides.takeaway: `value_or` is eager. Use it only with cheap defaults.

text.hook:
The config file does not exist.
The function returns an error message.
What does the caller see?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: C++23 std::expected. Both branches look right.

slides.title: The file is missing. What prints?

slides.verdict: A. loaded: config file not found
bullets: A plain `return x;` always constructs the **value**.
`E` and `T` are both `std::string`, so the message converts to `T` without complaint.
The error message became the config contents.
Only `return std::unexpected(...)` creates the error state.
slides.wrong: "B: returning the message from the error branch makes it an error"

slides.title: A distinct error type
slides.tip: Now `return ConfigError::NotFound;` without `unexpected` fails to compile instead of compiling wrongly.
slides.takeaway: In `std::expected`, success is implicit. Errors must be wrapped in `std::unexpected`.

text.hook:
The feature flag is explicitly set to false.
The code checks `if (enabled)`.
Ship it?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: `std::optional<bool>`: a three-state flag that reads like a two-state one.

slides.title:
The flag is off.
What does it print?

bullets: `if (enabled)` asks "is there a value?", not "is it true?".
slides.wrong: "A: `if (ob)` is fine because bool converts naturally"

slides.title: Spell the intent
slides.tip: `enabled == true` is false when empty, and false when it holds `false`.
slides.takeaway: For `optional<bool>`, the condition asks "is it set?", never "is it true?".

text.body: Two accessors look alike. Only one is checked.

slides.title:
The input is empty.
What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC 11, `-O0`: a different number each run. ASan + UBSan: silent
bullets: It reads whatever bytes are in the storage. No `int` lives there.
ASan sees valid stack memory, so it reports nothing.

slides.title: Check, or ask for the throw
slides.tip: Turn on `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` in debug and test builds: it makes `*opt` on empty abort.
slides.takeaway: `*opt` on empty is silent UB. `value()` is the checked accessor.
